pharm-cvs:cvmap.q: Nitrates relax vascular smooth muscle through:
pharm-cvs:cvmap.e: NO activates guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → myosin light chain dephosphorylation.

pharm-cvs:cvmap.q: Which class acts on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase?
pharm-cvs:cvmap.e: Digoxin inhibits the pump → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → ↑ Ca²⁺ via NCX.

pharm-cvs:cvmap.q: A 67-year-old woman with HFrEF is started on a new drug. Two weeks later she has a persistent dry cough, and serum K⁺ has risen from 4.4 to 5.3 mEq/L. Which mechanism best explains her cough?
pharm-cvs:cvmap.e: ACE (kininase II) inhibition raises bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema; hyperkalemia follows ↓ aldosterone. Neprilysin inhibitors are combined with ARBs, not used alone.

pharm-cvs:htn.q: First-line agent for hypertension in a patient with diabetes and albuminuria:

pharm-cvs:htn.e: Hydralazine is also used. RAAS inhibitors (ACEi, ARB, aliskiren) are teratogenic (renal dysgenesis).

pharm-cvs:htn.q: A 46-year-old man is started on hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure of 156/96 mm Hg. Six weeks later he wakes with an exquisitely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint; serum urate is 9.8 mg/dL. How did the drug most likely precipitate this?
pharm-cvs:htn.e: Thiazides cause volume contraction and compete for tubular urate secretion, raising serum urate. Xanthine oxidase inhibition would lower urate (allopurinol).

pharm-cvs:ccb.q: Which CCB class mainly acts on vascular smooth muscle?
pharm-cvs:ccb.e: Non-dihydropyridines act more on the heart (↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction).

pharm-cvs:ccb.q: A common adverse effect of dihydropyridine CCBs:
pharm-cvs:ccb.e: Also flushing, headache, gingival hyperplasia; verapamil causes constipation.

pharm-cvs:ccb.q: A 69-year-old man with hypertension and stable angina is started on a new drug. Three weeks later he reports constipation; HR is 54/min and the ECG shows a PR interval of 0.24 s. Which drug was most likely started?
pharm-cvs:ccb.e: Verapamil (non-dihydropyridine) slows SA/AV nodal conduction and causes constipation. Dihydropyridines cause reflex tachycardia and edema rather than AV block.

pharm-cvs:vasodil.e: Also reflex tachycardia; co-give a β-blocker. Used in pregnancy.
K⁺ channel opener in arterioles; reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.

pharm-cvs:vasodil.q: A 41-year-old woman treated for months with an arteriolar vasodilator for hypertension develops arthralgias, a malar rash and pleuritic chest pain. ANA and anti-histone antibodies are positive; anti-dsDNA is negative. Which patient factor most increased her risk?
pharm-cvs:vasodil.e: Hydralazine-induced lupus is more common in slow acetylators, who keep higher drug levels. TPMT deficiency predisposes to azathioprine/6-MP toxicity, not drug-induced lupus.

pharm-cvs:htnemerg.q: Which drug is used in hypertensive emergency and can cause cyanide toxicity?
pharm-cvs:htnemerg.e: Short acting; ↑cGMP via direct NO release.
Dilates renal vessels and promotes natriuresis; useful in hypertensive emergency with renal concerns.

pharm-cvs:htnemerg.q: A 58-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 210/120 mm Hg in the right arm and 170/100 mm Hg in the left, HR 108/min; CT angiography shows a type B aortic dissection. Which IV drug should be given first?
pharm-cvs:htnemerg.e: In aortic dissection, β-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) comes first to lower HR and dP/dt. Pure vasodilators given alone cause reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress.

pharm-cvs:nitrates.e: Reduced preload lowers myocardial O₂ demand.
Severe hypotension. Tolerance develops; need a nitrate-free interval.

pharm-cvs:nitrates.q: A 63-year-old man with stable angina has taken isosorbide dinitrate every 6 hours around the clock for 3 months. His angina, initially well controlled, has returned at the same dose. Which change is most appropriate?
o: Shorten the dosing to every 4 hours
pharm-cvs:nitrates.e: Continuous exposure causes nitrate tolerance; an 8–12 h nitrate-free interval restores efficacy. A 24-hour patch maintains exposure and worsens tolerance.

o: Blocking the If current in the SA node
Blocking β₁ receptors in the SA node
pharm-cvs:antianginal.e: ↓ diastolic wall tension; may prolong QT.

o: Blocking L-type Ca²⁺ channels in the AV node
Blocking β₁ receptors in the SA node
Blocking the If (funny) current in the SA node
Increasing vagal tone via M₂ receptors
pharm-cvs:antianginal.e: Used in HFrEF with HR ≥ 70 on maximal β-blocker; may cause luminous phenomena.

pharm-cvs:antianginal.q: A 66-year-old man has persistent exertional angina despite maximal metoprolol and amlodipine. Resting HR is 52/min and BP 102/64 mm Hg. A drug is added that reduces angina without lowering HR or BP. What is its mechanism?
o: Release of NO in venous smooth muscle
Inhibition of late inward Na⁺ current
Blockade of the If current in SA node
pharm-cvs:antianginal.e: Ranolazine inhibits the late Na⁺ current, reducing Ca²⁺ overload and diastolic wall tension without hemodynamic effects. Ivabradine (If block) would further lower an already slow HR.

pharm-cvs:hf.q: Which diuretic class reduces mortality in HFrEF?
Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate is especially beneficial in:
o: Patients with HFpEF and atrial fibrillation
pharm-cvs:hf.e: Also used when ACEi/ARB/ARNI are not tolerated.

pharm-cvs:hf.q: A 63-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 30%) takes lisinopril, metoprolol succinate, furosemide and spironolactone. He develops painful bilateral breast enlargement. Which drug is the most appropriate substitute to keep the mortality benefit?
pharm-cvs:hf.e: Spironolactone's antiandrogen effect causes gynecomastia; eplerenone is a more selective MRA that also reduces HFrEF mortality. Amiloride spares K⁺ but has no proven HF mortality benefit.

pharm-cvs:digoxin.e: Low K⁺ increases digoxin binding to the pump; also renal failure and verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine.

pharm-cvs:digoxin.q: Classic ECG/vision signs of digoxin toxicity:
o: Delta waves, short PR interval, wide QRS
pharm-cvs:digoxin.e: Nausea, blurry yellow vision, AV block; worse with renal failure and hypokalemia.

pharm-cvs:digoxin.q: A 76-year-old woman with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation has a ventricular rate of 118/min and BP 92/58 mm Hg. A drug is added that increases contractility and also slows the ventricular rate. By which mechanism does it slow AV conduction?
o: ↑ Vagal tone at the AV node
K⁺ channel block in nodal tissue
β₁ blockade at the AV node
L-type Ca²⁺ block in the AV node
pharm-cvs:digoxin.e: Digoxin's parasympathomimetic (vagal) effect slows AV nodal conduction; its inotropy comes from Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition. β-blockers and CCBs would lower BP and contractility further.

pharm-cvs:statins.e: Myopathy risk rises with fibrates, niacin and CYP3A4 inhibitors.

pharm-cvs:statins.q: A 52-year-old woman with LDL 182 mg/dL is started on a drug that inhibits the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis. Eight weeks later her LDL is 96 mg/dL. Which change chiefly accounts for the fall in plasma LDL?
pharm-cvs:statins.e: Statins lower hepatocyte cholesterol, activating SREBP-2 to upregulate LDL receptors that clear LDL. Reduced intestinal absorption is the mechanism of ezetimibe.

pharm-cvs:nonstatin.e: Blocks cholesterol absorption at the brush border → lowers LDL; well tolerated.
Also impair absorption of other drugs and fat-soluble vitamins; GI upset.

pharm-cvs:nonstatin.q: A 42-year-old man with familial hypercholesterolemia has tendon xanthomas and LDL 190 mg/dL despite maximal atorvastatin plus ezetimibe. He starts a subcutaneous monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks. What is its mechanism?
o: Inhibits MTP to block VLDL assembly
pharm-cvs:nonstatin.e: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) stop PCSK9 from targeting LDL receptors for lysosomal degradation. NPC1L1 is ezetimibe's target, already on board.

pharm-cvs:tg.e: Best for lowering TG; risk of gallstones and myopathy with statins.
Prostaglandin-mediated; niacin can also cause hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia.

pharm-cvs:tg.q: A 47-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes was admitted last month for acute pancreatitis. Fasting triglycerides are 1,150 mg/dL; LDL is 110 mg/dL. Which drug is most appropriate to lower his risk of recurrence?
pharm-cvs:tg.e: Fibrates (PPAR-α → ↑ lipoprotein lipase) are the most effective TG-lowering drugs. Bile acid resins such as colesevelam can raise triglycerides.

pharm-cvs:class1.q: Which class I agent is used for ventricular arrhythmias after MI?
Class IC drugs are contraindicated in:

A 64-year-old man is treated with a class IA antiarrhythmic for atrial fibrillation. Two weeks later he has tinnitus, headache, blurred vision and diarrhea, and his QTc has lengthened. Which drug is he most likely taking?
pharm-cvs:class1.e: Cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, visual and GI upset) is characteristic of quinidine. Procainamide is also class IA but is known for drug-induced lupus, not cinchonism.

pharm-cvs:class2.q: β-blockers slow conduction mainly at the:
pharm-cvs:class2.e: ↓ Phase 4 slope and ↑ PR interval in nodal tissue. Esmolol is very short acting; metoprolol is used for rate control.
Nonselective agents worsen bronchospasm; may mask hypoglycemia.

pharm-cvs:class2.q: A 60-year-old man with type 1 diabetes starts propranolol after a myocardial infarction. A week later he is found confused with capillary glucose 42 mg/dL and says he never felt shaky or had palpitations. Why were his warning symptoms absent?
pharm-cvs:class2.e: β-blockers mask adrenergic hypoglycemia symptoms (tremor, palpitations) and nonselective agents also blunt glycogenolysis. They do not stimulate insulin secretion.

pharm-cvs:class3.e: Also hepatotoxicity. Check PFTs, LFTs and TFTs; blue-gray skin and corneal deposits.

pharm-cvs:class3.q: Class III agents prolong the action potential by blocking:
pharm-cvs:class3.e: Prolong QT; sotalol and dofetilide carry torsades risk.

pharm-cvs:class3.q: A 68-year-old man on long-term antiarrhythmic therapy has 3 months of dry cough and dyspnea with bibasal crackles; CT shows reticular opacities and DLCO is reduced. He also has blue-gray facial skin and TSH 11 mU/L. Which drug is most likely responsible?
pharm-cvs:class3.e: Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (iodine content) and blue-gray skin. Sotalol and dofetilide mainly cause QT prolongation/torsades.

pharm-cvs:class4.q: Adenosine is the drug of choice to terminate:
pharm-cvs:class4.e: Very short acting; causes flushing, chest pain; effect blocked by theophylline/caffeine.

pharm-cvs:class4.q: A 27-year-old woman has palpitations; HR is 186/min with a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia and BP 118/74 mm Hg. Vagal maneuvers fail. A rapid IV bolus causes brief flushing and chest tightness, then sinus rhythm returns. What is this drug's mechanism?
o: A₁ receptor → K⁺ efflux at AV node
Block of K⁺ channels → long ERP
Block of L-type Ca²⁺ at AV node
Block of β₁ receptors at AV node
pharm-cvs:class4.e: Adenosine acts on A₁ (Gi) receptors, ↑ K⁺ efflux and ↓ Ca²⁺ current, transiently blocking the AV node. Verapamil blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels and acts more slowly.

o: Reduce HF admissions and CV death
pharm-cvs:hfrx.e: Benefit is seen with or without diabetes. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin are one of the four pillars.

pharm-cvs:hfrx.q: Before starting an ARNI in a patient on an ACE inhibitor, stop the ACEi for:

A 59-year-old woman without diabetes has HFrEF (EF 32%) on sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol and spironolactone. A fourth drug is added; two months later she develops vulvovaginal candidiasis. What is the added drug's mechanism?
o: Blocks the If current in the SA node
pharm-cvs:hfrx.e: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) cause glucosuria, predisposing to genital mycotic infections, and reduce HF death/admission even without diabetes. Neprilysin is already inhibited by sacubitril.

cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.q: The main determinant of prognosis and degree of cyanosis in tetralogy of Fallot is:
o: Size of the ventricular septal defect
cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.e: Pulmonary infundibular stenosis decides how much blood shunts right to left across the VSD.

cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.q: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failure of:
cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.e: The truncus never divides into aorta and pulmonary trunk; a VSD is almost always present.

cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.q: A newborn of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes becomes deeply cyanotic within hours of birth. Chest x-ray shows a narrow superior mediastinum ('egg on a string') and echo shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle. Which therapy keeps him alive until surgery?
cvs-patho-1:chd-rl.e: D-TGA creates two parallel circuits; PGE1 keeps the ductus open so the circulations can mix.

cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.q: In a ventricular septal defect, oxygen saturation first increases in the:
cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.e: Oxygenated LV blood enters the RV, so the step-up appears in the RV and pulmonary artery.

cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.q: A wide, fixed split S2 is characteristic of:
cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.e: Extra RV volume delays pulmonic closure and the split does not vary with respiration.

cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.q: A 2-day-old premature infant whose mother had fever and a rash in the first trimester has a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle and bounding pulses. Which drug is most likely to close the lesion?
cvs-patho-1:chd-lr.e: Patent ductus arteriosus (congenital rubella association); prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors close it, PGE1 keeps it open.

cvs-patho-1:eisen.q: Eisenmenger syndrome develops when an uncorrected left-to-right shunt causes:
o: Systemic hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy
Spontaneous closure of the defect by fibrous tissue
Left ventricular failure with a reduced ejection fraction
Pulmonary vascular remodeling until RV pressure exceeds LV
cvs-patho-1:eisen.e: Raised pulmonary flow remodels the arterioles; PVR rises and the shunt reverses.

cvs-patho-1:eisen.q: Which finding is expected once Eisenmenger syndrome develops?
cvs-patho-1:eisen.e: Chronic hypoxemia drives erythropoietin release; clubbing and late cyanosis also occur.

cvs-patho-1:eisen.q: A 28-year-old woman with a murmur since childhood that was never treated now has exertional dyspnea, cyanosis and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. Which untreated lesion is most likely?
cvs-patho-1:eisen.e: A reversed PDA delivers deoxygenated blood into the aorta beyond the arm vessels: differential cyanosis.

cvs-patho-1:coarct.q: Rib notching in adult coarctation is caused by:
o: Erosion from a dilated aortic arch
cvs-patho-1:coarct.e: Internal thoracic → intercostal collaterals bypass the narrowing and erode the inferior rib margins.

cvs-patho-1:coarct.q: Coarctation of the aorta is most strongly associated with which syndrome?
cvs-patho-1:coarct.e: Turner syndrome: coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.

cvs-patho-1:coarct.q: A 16-year-old boy has headaches and leg cramps when running. BP is 168/96 mm Hg in the right arm; femoral pulses are weak and delayed and a systolic murmur is heard over the back. Which associated valve abnormality should be sought?
cvs-patho-1:coarct.e: Adult coarctation often coexists with a bicuspid aortic valve.

cvs-patho-1:chd-assoc.q: Prenatal lithium exposure is associated with:
cvs-patho-1:chd-assoc.e: Downward displacement of the tricuspid leaflets.

cvs-patho-1:chd-assoc.q: Supravalvular aortic stenosis is characteristic of:

A 3-month-old with a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease feeds poorly and has a holosystolic murmur. Echo shows a common atrioventricular valve. The defect arises from abnormal development of the:
cvs-patho-1:chd-assoc.e: Down syndrome is most associated with atrioventricular septal defects.

cvs-patho-1:htn.q: By the definition used in First Aid, hypertension is a persistent blood pressure of at least:
A 'string of beads' renal artery in a young woman indicates:
cvs-patho-1:htn.e: Alternating webs and dilations; a cause of renovascular hypertension.

cvs-patho-1:htn.q: A 38-year-old man has BP 158/98 mm Hg despite three drugs including a diuretic. K⁺ is 3.1 mEq/L and plasma renin is suppressed. The most likely cause of his hypertension is:
cvs-patho-1:htn.e: Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and low renin points to autonomous aldosterone secretion.

cvs-patho-1:htn-organ.q: What distinguishes hypertensive emergency from hypertensive urgency?
o: A diastolic pressure above 120 mm Hg
A systolic pressure above 200 mm Hg
cvs-patho-1:htn-organ.e: Both have severe BP; only emergency has acute organ damage.

cvs-patho-1:htn-organ.q: Arterioles in hypertensive emergency characteristically show:

A 50-year-old man with untreated hypertension has headache, confusion and blurred vision. BP is 230/130 mm Hg, fundoscopy shows papilledema and flame hemorrhages, and creatinine has risen. Initial treatment should lower mean arterial pressure by about:
o: 25% over the first hours with an IV agent
To normal within 1 hour with oral clonidine
cvs-patho-1:htn-organ.e: Hypertensive emergency: controlled IV reduction avoids cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion.

cvs-patho-1:lipid.q: Xanthomas of the Achilles tendon most strongly suggest:
cvs-patho-1:lipid.e: LDL receptor defects cause tendinous xanthomas.
Foamy macrophages form yellow eyelid plaques.

cvs-patho-1:lipid.q: A 24-year-old man has a white ring around the edge of both corneas and firm nodules over his knuckle tendons. His father died of MI at 42. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely?
cvs-patho-1:lipid.e: Early corneal arcus + tendon xanthomas = familial hypercholesterolemia.

cvs-patho-1:athero.q: Which growth factor mediates smooth muscle migration into the intima in atherosclerosis?
cvs-patho-1:athero.e: PDGF (and FGF) recruit and stimulate smooth muscle cells to form the fibrous cap.

cvs-patho-1:athero.q: The most common site of atherosclerosis is the:
cvs-patho-1:athero.e: Abdominal aorta > coronary > popliteal > carotid > circle of Willis.

cvs-patho-1:athero.q: A 62-year-old smoker dies suddenly. Autopsy shows a coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and an overlying occlusive thrombus. The event that most directly precipitated the thrombus was:
cvs-patho-1:athero.e: Cap rupture exposes thrombogenic core contents to blood.

cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.q: Cholesterol emboli syndrome most often follows:
cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.e: Catheters and endovascular devices dislodge atheromatous debris.

cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.q: On biopsy, cholesterol emboli appear as:
cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.e: Crystals dissolve during processing and leave biconvex clefts.

cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.q: Two weeks after coronary angiography, a 70-year-old man has rising creatinine, a lacy purple rash on the legs and painful bluish toes. Pedal pulses are palpable. Which mechanism is most likely?
cvs-patho-1:chol-emb.e: Livedo, blue toes and AKI with intact pulses after a vascular procedure.

cvs-patho-1:arteriolo.q: Onion-skin thickening of arterioles is typical of:
cvs-patho-1:arteriolo.e: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, often with fibrinoid necrosis.
Calcification of the media of muscular arteries; usually asymptomatic.

cvs-patho-1:arteriolo.q: A 66-year-old woman with 20 years of type 2 diabetes has proteinuria. Kidney biopsy shows homogeneous pink thickening of both afferent and efferent arteriolar walls. This change is:
cvs-patho-1:arteriolo.e: Plasma protein leak plus matrix; diabetes affects both arterioles.

cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.q: The strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm is:
cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.e: Smoking, male sex, age and family history.

cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.q: Cystic medial degeneration underlies aneurysms of the:
cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.e: Thoracic aneurysms: hypertension, bicuspid valve, Marfan.

cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.q: A 72-year-old man who smoked for 50 years collapses with severe back pain. BP is 70/40 mm Hg and a pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. The lesion most likely lies:
cvs-patho-1:aneurysm.e: Ruptured AAA; most are infrarenal where vasa vasorum are sparse.

cvs-patho-1:dissection.q: The strongest risk factor for aortic dissection is:
cvs-patho-1:dissection.e: Hypertension stresses the media; connective tissue disorders and bicuspid valves also predispose.

cvs-patho-1:dissection.q: Stanford type A dissection is defined by involvement of the:
cvs-patho-1:dissection.e: Type A: ascending aorta (surgery); type B: descending only.

cvs-patho-1:dissection.q: A 45-year-old tall man with long fingers and lens dislocation has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a new diastolic murmur. BP differs by 30 mm Hg between the arms. The best management after imaging confirms the lesion is:
cvs-patho-1:dissection.e: Marfan syndrome with type A dissection and acute aortic regurgitation.

cvs-patho-1:subclavian.q: In subclavian steal, blood flow is reversed in the:
cvs-patho-1:subclavian.e: Blood runs down the vertebral artery to supply the arm beyond the stenosis.

o: Turning the head to the left

cvs-patho-1:subclavian.q: A 67-year-old smoker becomes dizzy whenever he paints a ceiling with his left arm. Left arm BP is 118/70 mm Hg and right arm 146/82 mm Hg. The lesion is most likely located:
o: In the left subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral artery
In the brachiocephalic trunk distal to its branches
In the left common carotid artery bifurcation
In the left vertebral artery near the basilar junction
cvs-patho-1:subclavian.e: Proximal subclavian stenosis (usually atherosclerosis) causes steal.

cvs-patho-1:vwall.q: The stereotyped response of a vessel wall to injury is:
o: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation with matrix
cvs-patho-1:vwall.e: Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima, proliferate and deposit ECM.

o: Complete loss of endothelial cells over an atheroma
Loss of normal endothelial functions without visible damage
Calcification of the internal elastic lamina in the media
Thrombus formation on a denuded intimal surface
cvs-patho-1:vwall.e: For example reduced NO and increased adhesion molecules.

cvs-patho-1:vwall.q: Six months after coronary stent placement, a 58-year-old man has recurrent angina. Angiography shows narrowing within the stent. The main tissue causing restenosis is:
o: Neointima of proliferating smooth muscle cells
cvs-patho-1:vwall.e: In-stent restenosis is intimal hyperplasia — the healing response.

o: Loss of NO from endothelial cells
Increased ENaC activity in collecting ducts
Excess aldosterone from an adrenal adenoma
cvs-patho-1:bp-reg.e: Gain-of-function of the epithelial Na⁺ channel.

cvs-patho-1:bp-reg.q: Blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by:
A 26-year-old man has hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Renin and aldosterone are both low, and amiloride normalizes his BP while spironolactone does not. The defect involves:
o: Gain of function of the epithelial Na⁺ channel
cvs-patho-1:bp-reg.e: Liddle syndrome: ENaC overactivity independent of aldosterone.

cvs-patho-2:cad.q: Unstable angina differs from NSTEMI by the absence of:
cvs-patho-2:cad.e: Both can have rest pain and ST depression; only NSTEMI has myocardial necrosis.

cvs-patho-2:cad.q: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina is best treated with:
cvs-patho-2:cad.e: Relax coronary smooth muscle and stop smoking; nonselective β-blockers can worsen spasm.

cvs-patho-2:cad.q: A 59-year-old man has had chest pain at rest for 40 minutes. ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6, and troponin is elevated on two measurements. The infarct most likely involves:
o: The full thickness of the wall
cvs-patho-2:cad.e: NSTEMI = subendocardial infarction, the zone farthest from epicardial flow.

cvs-patho-2:steal.q: Coronary steal occurs with vasodilators because vessels distal to a stenosis are:
cvs-patho-2:steal.e: Only normal vessels can dilate further, so flow is diverted toward them.

cvs-patho-2:steal.q: Which drug is used for pharmacologic stress testing based on coronary steal?
cvs-patho-2:steal.e: Adenosine A2A agonist vasodilator (also adenosine, dipyridamole).

cvs-patho-2:steal.q: During a dipyridamole stress test, a 64-year-old woman with a 90% circumflex stenosis develops chest pain and lateral ST depression. Why does a vasodilator provoke ischemia?
o: The drug constricts the stenotic segment
Flow is diverted to normally responsive vessels
It causes platelet aggregation at the plaque
It increases myocardial oxygen demand directly
cvs-patho-2:steal.e: Coronary steal: post-stenotic beds are already maximally dilated.

cvs-patho-2:scd.q: The most common cause of sudden cardiac death is:
cvs-patho-2:scd.e: Up to 70% of cases; usually via ventricular fibrillation.

cvs-patho-2:scd.q: Myocardial hibernation is best described as:
o: Brief dysfunction after a short ischemic episode
Permanent loss of contractility from scar tissue
cvs-patho-2:scd.e: Stunning is the transient dysfunction after brief ischemia; both are reversible.

cvs-patho-2:scd.q: A 38-year-old man collapses while jogging and cannot be resuscitated. He had no symptoms beforehand. The immediate mechanism of death was most likely:
cvs-patho-2:scd.e: Sudden cardiac death is usually a lethal ventricular arrhythmia.

cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.q: Neutrophilic infiltration of an infarct is most prominent at about:
cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.e: Then macrophages (3–10 days), granulation tissue, and scar.

cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.q: Contraction band necrosis is characteristic of:
o: Remote infarct with dense collagen scar
cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.e: Ca²⁺ influx on reperfusion causes hypercontraction of myofibrils.

cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.q: A 66-year-old man dies 6 days after an anterior MI. Histology of the infarct border would most likely show:
o: Dense collagenous scar with few cells
cvs-patho-2:mi-evo.e: At 3–7 days macrophages phagocytose dead cells; the wall is soft and rupture-prone.

cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.q: Which marker is most useful for detecting reinfarction 4 days after an MI?
cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.e: CK-MB returns to normal in about 48 hours; troponin stays high 7–10 days.

cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.q: Cardiac troponin I usually remains elevated for:
cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.e: Rises after ~4 h and peaks at ~24 h.

cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.q: A 61-year-old woman had an MI 5 days ago and now has new chest pain. Her troponin I is still elevated from the first event. Which test best shows a new infarction?
cvs-patho-2:mi-dx.e: A fresh CK-MB rise indicates reinfarction.

cvs-patho-2:ecg-loc.q: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF indicates occlusion of the:
ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves suggests infarction of the:
cvs-patho-2:ecg-loc.e: Mirror image of posterior ST elevation; confirm with V7–V9.

cvs-patho-2:ecg-loc.q: A 54-year-old man has crushing chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in V1–V4. Which artery is most likely occluded?

cvs-patho-2:narrow.q: The most common site of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation is the:
cvs-patho-2:narrow.e: Stasis in the LA appendage causes embolic stroke.

cvs-patho-2:narrow.q: A short PR interval with a delta wave indicates:
cvs-patho-2:narrow.e: An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) pre-excites the ventricle.

cvs-patho-2:narrow.q: A 72-year-old woman with a COPD exacerbation has an irregularly irregular rhythm at 130/min. The ECG shows at least three different P-wave morphologies. Diagnosis?
cvs-patho-2:narrow.e: Multiple atrial ectopic foci; treat the lung disease.

cvs-patho-2:wide.q: Brugada syndrome is most commonly due to a mutation in a:
cvs-patho-2:wide.e: Autosomal dominant loss of function of the cardiac Na⁺ channel.

cvs-patho-2:wide.q: The treatment of torsades de pointes in a hemodynamically stable patient is:
cvs-patho-2:wide.e: Amiodarone and procainamide prolong QT; unstable patients need defibrillation.

cvs-patho-2:wide.q: A 6-year-old girl with congenital sensorineural deafness faints when startled. ECG shows a QTc of 560 ms. Her parents hear normally. The disorder is:
cvs-patho-2:wide.e: Congenital long QT with deafness, recessive inheritance.

cvs-patho-2:blocks.q: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped describes:
Which conduction abnormality usually requires a pacemaker?
cvs-patho-2:blocks.e: Infranodal disease that may progress to complete block.

cvs-patho-2:blocks.q: A 44-year-old hiker from Connecticut with a recent expanding red rash has syncope. ECG shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular QRS complexes at 38/min with no relationship between them. Diagnosis:
o: First-degree AV block from digoxin use
Sick sinus syndrome from SA node aging
Third-degree AV block from Lyme carditis
Mobitz I block from high vagal tone
cvs-patho-2:blocks.e: AV dissociation after erythema migrans: Lyme carditis.

cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.q: Papillary muscle rupture after MI most often involves the posteromedial muscle because it:
o: Is supplied by the LAD alone
Is thinner than the anterolateral muscle
Has a single blood supply from the PDA
cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.e: The anterolateral muscle has dual supply (LAD and LCX).

cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.q: A pseudoaneurysm differs from a true ventricular aneurysm because it:
o: Contains all three layers of the wall
Is contained only by pericardium or scar
cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.e: It is a contained rupture and is more likely to rupture.

cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.q: Five days after an anterior MI, a 68-year-old man develops sudden hypotension and a new loud holosystolic murmur. Right heart catheterization shows an O₂ saturation step-up in the right ventricle. Diagnosis:
cvs-patho-2:mi-comp.e: Acute VSD from macrophage-mediated degradation at 3–5 days.

cvs-patho-2:acs.q: For STEMI, primary PCI is preferred if it can be done within about:
cvs-patho-2:acs.e: Otherwise give fibrinolysis if there is no contraindication.

cvs-patho-2:acs.q: In a right ventricular infarction, which drug should be avoided?
cvs-patho-2:acs.e: The RV is preload-dependent; nitrates can cause profound hypotension.

cvs-patho-2:acs.q: A 57-year-old man has 2 hours of chest pain, ST elevation in II, III and aVF, and BP 82/50 mm Hg with clear lungs and a raised JVP. Besides emergency PCI, what should be given?
cvs-patho-2:acs.e: Inferior MI with RV involvement: support preload.

cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.q: Most acute coronary syndromes start from a plaque that:
o: Calcifies completely and becomes rigid and stable
Is disrupted acutely, often with only modest stenosis
Slowly enlarges until it finally occludes the lumen
cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.e: Acute plaque change (rupture, erosion, hemorrhage) then thrombosis.

cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.q: Which feature makes a plaque vulnerable to rupture?
o: Thin fibrous cap over a large lipid core
Small lipid core with many SMCs
Thick collagenous cap with few cells
cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.e: Inflammation and MMPs thin the cap.

cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.q: A 60-year-old man's occluded LAD is opened by PCI 3 hours after onset. Tissue from the reperfused zone would most likely show:
o: Dense collagen scar with few nuclei
cvs-patho-2:ihd-path.e: Reperfusion injury: bleeding through damaged vessels and hypercontracted myofibrils.

cvs-patho-2:af-care.q: In CHA₂DS₂-VASc, which factors score 2 points each?
For anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation with a mechanical heart valve, the drug of choice is:
cvs-patho-2:af-care.e: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.

cvs-patho-2:af-care.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has newly found nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and no bleeding history. The most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent stroke is:

cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.q: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most often caused by mutations in genes for:
cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.e: β-myosin heavy chain and myosin-binding protein C; autosomal dominant.

cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.q: Which drugs should be avoided in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy?
cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.e: Reducing preload or afterload worsens outflow obstruction.

cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.q: A 34-year-old woman develops progressive dyspnea 1 month after delivering her first child. Echo shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%. The pattern of hypertrophy is:
cvs-patho-3:cardiomyo.e: Peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy: eccentric hypertrophy with systolic dysfunction.

cvs-patho-3:hf.q: 'Heart failure cells' in the lungs are:
cvs-patho-3:hf.e: Alveolar macrophages that ingested RBCs leaked from congested capillaries.

cvs-patho-3:hf.q: Which therapy improves survival in HFrEF?
cvs-patho-3:hf.e: Also ACEi/ARB/ARNI, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors; loops relieve symptoms only.

cvs-patho-3:hf.q: A 58-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has dyspnea and orthopnea. Echo shows a thick, small LV with an ejection fraction of 62% and impaired relaxation. The mechanism of his heart failure is:
cvs-patho-3:hf.e: HFpEF: stiff hypertrophied ventricle raises filling pressure.

cvs-patho-3:shock.q: Which shock type has decreased SVR as the primary disturbance?
In cardiogenic shock, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is:
cvs-patho-3:shock.e: Blood backs up behind the failing left ventricle.

cvs-patho-3:shock.q: A 24-year-old man is stung by a bee and becomes hypotensive with warm, flushed skin. Which hemodynamic pattern is expected?

cvs-patho-3:tamponade.q: Beck triad consists of hypotension, distended neck veins and:
Electrical alternans on ECG is caused by:
o: Swinging of the heart in a large effusion
cvs-patho-3:tamponade.e: The electrical axis shifts as the heart moves in the fluid.

cvs-patho-3:tamponade.q: A 45-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer has dyspnea. BP is 86/60 mm Hg, JVP is raised and systolic BP drops 18 mm Hg on inspiration. Echo would most likely show:
o: Dilated left ventricle with low EF
Diastolic collapse of the right ventricle
Systolic anterior motion of mitral leaflet
cvs-patho-3:tamponade.e: Malignant pericardial effusion with tamponade and pulsus paradoxus.

cvs-patho-3:syncope.q: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall within 3 minutes of standing of:
The most common type of syncope is:
cvs-patho-3:syncope.e: Prodrome of warmth, pallor and nausea; quick recovery.

cvs-patho-3:syncope.q: A 76-year-old man faints while climbing stairs. He has had exertional chest tightness, and a crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur radiates to the carotids. This syncope is:
cvs-patho-3:syncope.e: Aortic stenosis limits cardiac output during exertion.

cvs-patho-3:ie.q: Tricuspid valve endocarditis is most associated with:
cvs-patho-3:ie.e: S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida; septic emboli go to the lungs.

cvs-patho-3:ie.q: Painful raised lesions on the finger pads in endocarditis are:
cvs-patho-3:ie.e: Immunologic phenomenon ('Ouchy'); Janeway lesions are painless.

cvs-patho-3:ie.q: A 74-year-old man has fever for 3 weeks and a new mitral regurgitation murmur. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. The next most important evaluation is:
cvs-patho-3:ie.e: S. gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis is associated with colon cancer.

cvs-patho-3:rheumatic.q: Rheumatic fever is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
cvs-patho-3:rheumatic.e: Antibodies to M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin.

cvs-patho-3:rheumatic.q: Anitschkow cells in rheumatic carditis are:

A 35-year-old woman from a low-income country has dyspnea, hemoptysis and atrial fibrillation. An opening snap is followed by a diastolic rumble at the apex. The valve lesion most likely resulted from:
cvs-patho-3:rheumatic.e: Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic.

cvs-patho-3:valves.q: The most common cause of aortic stenosis in older adults is:
cvs-patho-3:valves.e: Calcified masses on the outflow side of the cusps; earlier with bicuspid valves.

cvs-patho-3:valves.q: A midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur indicates:
cvs-patho-3:valves.e: Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral leaflets.

cvs-patho-3:valves.q: A 68-year-old man has exertional syncope and angina. His carotid pulse is weak and delayed. The left ventricle most likely shows:

cvs-patho-3:pericard.q: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG suggests:
cvs-patho-3:pericard.e: Concave ST elevation in many leads not matching a coronary territory.
The RV cannot accept the inspiratory increase in venous return.

cvs-patho-3:pericard.q: A 50-year-old man from a TB-endemic region has edema, ascites and a raised JVP that increases on inspiration. CXR shows pericardial calcification and an early diastolic sound is heard. Diagnosis:
cvs-patho-3:pericard.e: Pericardial knock, Kussmaul sign and calcification.

cvs-patho-3:myocarditis.q: Which clinical finding is characteristic of myocarditis?
o: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
cvs-patho-3:myocarditis.e: Also arrhythmias and heart failure; a major cause of SCD under 40.
Parasites within myocytes; later dilated cardiomyopathy.

cvs-patho-3:myocarditis.q: A 22-year-old man has chest pain, dyspnea and tachycardia 10 days after a flu-like illness. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Endomyocardial biopsy would most likely show:

cvs-patho-3:hht.q: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is inherited as:
A high-flow arteriovenous malformation can lead to:

A 40-year-old woman has had recurrent nosebleeds since childhood, blanching red spots on her lips and tongue, and iron-deficiency anemia. Her mother had similar problems. Imaging is most important to screen for:
o: Berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
cvs-patho-3:hht.e: HHT causes AVMs in lung, brain and liver.

cvs-patho-3:tumors.q: The most common primary cardiac tumor in adults is:
cvs-patho-3:tumors.e: Usually in the left atrium; metastases are more common overall.
Most common primary cardiac tumor in children.

cvs-patho-3:tumors.q: A 45-year-old woman has fever, weight loss and fainting episodes when she sits up. A low-pitched early diastolic sound is heard. Echo shows a pedunculated mass in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum. Histology would show:
o: Stellate cells in a myxoid matrix
cvs-patho-3:tumors.e: Myxoma with ball-valve obstruction ('tumor plop'); IL-6 causes constitutional symptoms.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-large.q: Jaw claudication in an older adult suggests:
cvs-patho-3:vasc-large.e: Granulomatous inflammation of temporal and other cranial branches.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-large.q: A 72-year-old woman has a new right-sided headache, scalp tenderness and transient blurred vision in the right eye. ESR is 96 mm/h. The best next step is:
cvs-patho-3:vasc-large.e: Giant cell arteritis threatens permanent blindness; biopsy can follow treatment.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-med.e: Medium arteries of kidney, gut, nerves and skin.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-med.q: The most serious complication of Kawasaki disease is:
A 47-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has fever, weight loss, abdominal pain after meals, new hypertension and foot drop. ANCA is negative. Angiography would most likely show:
o: Narrowing of the aortic arch branches
Smooth tapering of the temporal arteries
Microaneurysms of renal and mesenteric arteries

cvs-patho-3:vasc-small.e: Upper airway, lung and kidney involvement with granulomas.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-small.q: Microscopic polyangiitis differs from GPA by the absence of:
cvs-patho-3:vasc-small.e: MPA is p-ANCA (MPO) positive and lacks granulomas.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-small.q: A 7-year-old boy has palpable purpura on his buttocks and legs, knee pain and colicky abdominal pain 2 weeks after a cold. Urinalysis shows hematuria. Deposits in his vessels contain:

cvs-patho-3:vasc-tumor.e: Seen in AIDS, transplant recipients and older Mediterranean men.

cvs-patho-3:vasc-tumor.q: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to:
A man with advanced HIV has multiple red-purple skin papules. Biopsy shows proliferating vessels with many neutrophils and clumps of bacilli on silver stain. The lesions should be treated with:

cvs-physio-1:cov.q: Phosphorylation of phospholamban by protein kinase A increases contractility mainly by:
o: Increasing troponin C affinity for Ca²⁺ directly
Blocking the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger in the sarcolemma
Opening fast Na⁺ channels during phase 0
Relieving inhibition of SERCA so the SR stores more Ca²⁺
cvs-physio-1:cov.e: PKA-phosphorylated phospholamban no longer inhibits SERCA2a: faster Ca²⁺ reuptake (relaxation) and a larger SR Ca²⁺ store for the next beat.

cvs-physio-1:cov.q: Digoxin raises intracellular Ca²⁺ in cardiac myocytes because it:
o: Opens L-type Ca²⁺ channels during the plateau
Activates β₁ receptors and raises cAMP levels
cvs-physio-1:cov.e: Higher intracellular Na⁺ lowers the gradient that drives Ca²⁺ extrusion through NCX.

cvs-physio-1:cov.q: A 66-year-old man with stable angina is started on verapamil. Which change in the ventricular myocyte explains the drop in his stroke volume at a constant preload and afterload?
o: More Ca²⁺ reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Faster K⁺ efflux through delayed rectifier channels
Less Na⁺ entry through fast channels during phase 0
Less Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels during the plateau
cvs-physio-1:cov.e: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs reduce L-type Ca²⁺ influx, so less trigger Ca²⁺ for Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release → negative inotropy.

cvs-physio-1:o2d.q: By Laplace's law, wall stress of the left ventricle increases when:
o: Wall thickness increases at the same pressure
Ventricular pressure falls at the same radius
Chamber radius increases at the same pressure
Heart rate falls with no change in geometry
cvs-physio-1:o2d.e: Wall stress = P × r / 2h; a larger radius raises stress, a thicker wall lowers it.

cvs-physio-1:o2d.q: The blood with the lowest O₂ content in the body is normally found in the:
cvs-physio-1:o2d.e: Myocardium extracts a very high fraction of delivered O₂ even at rest.

cvs-physio-1:o2d.q: A 58-year-old woman has long-standing untreated hypertension. Echocardiography shows a thick-walled LV with a normal cavity size. This remodeling primarily serves to:
o: Normalize wall stress against the higher pressure
Reduce heart rate and diastolic filling time
Increase chamber radius to raise stroke volume
cvs-physio-1:o2d.e: Concentric hypertrophy raises wall thickness (h), offsetting the higher P in P·r/2h.

cvs-physio-1:coeq.q: A ventricle has EDV 150 mL and ESV 90 mL. Its ejection fraction is:
Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to:
cvs-physio-1:coeq.e: Stiffer arteries (lower compliance) widen pulse pressure for the same stroke volume.

cvs-physio-1:coeq.q: A patient consumes 300 mL O₂/min. Arterial O₂ content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous O₂ content is 140 mL/L. His cardiac output is:
A 30-year-old man has BP 130/70 mm Hg at a resting heart rate. His mean arterial pressure is closest to:

cvs-physio-1:starling.q: The Frank–Starling relationship states that stroke volume rises with:
cvs-physio-1:starling.e: Greater preload stretches sarcomeres toward optimal overlap and raises Ca²⁺ sensitivity.

cvs-physio-1:starling.q: A positive inotrope shifts the Starling curve so that, at the same EDV, stroke volume is:
cvs-physio-1:starling.e: Inotropes move the whole curve upward.

cvs-physio-1:starling.q: A 70-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy receives dobutamine in the ICU. Compared with before the infusion, his ventricle now operates on:
o: A lower Starling curve, with less SV at the same preload
The descending limb of the same Starling curve
A higher Starling curve, with more SV at the same preload
The same Starling curve, at a much higher preload
cvs-physio-1:starling.e: β₁ agonism increases contractility, shifting the curve up.

cvs-physio-1:flow.q: If arteriolar radius falls by half and all else is constant, resistance increases about:
Three identical vascular beds arranged in parallel have a total resistance equal to:
o: One third of one bed's resistance
The same as one bed's resistance

cvs-physio-1:flow.q: A 64-year-old man with polycythemia vera has a hematocrit of 62%. Compared with normal, flow through a vessel at the same pressure gradient is:
o: Decreased, because vessel length is increased
cvs-physio-1:flow.e: Viscosity depends mostly on hematocrit; higher η raises resistance (8ηL/πr⁴).

cvs-physio-1:vtree.q: Blood flow velocity is lowest in the capillaries because they have the:
o: Thinnest walls of any blood vessel
cvs-physio-1:vtree.e: v = Q/A; capillaries have the largest combined area (~2500 cm²).

cvs-physio-1:vtree.q: The largest drop in mean pressure along the systemic circulation occurs across the:
A trauma patient loses 700 mL of blood. Which vascular compartment held most of the circulating blood volume before the injury?
cvs-physio-1:vtree.e: About 64% of blood volume is in systemic veins (capacitance vessels).

cvs-physio-1:vfc.q: On a cardiac and vascular function curve diagram, the x-intercept of the venous return curve equals the:
cvs-physio-1:vfc.e: VR is zero when RAP equals MSFP (~7 mm Hg).

cvs-physio-1:vfc.q: A rapid saline infusion shifts the venous return curve:
cvs-physio-1:vfc.e: Volume (or venous tone) changes MSFP without changing the slope.

cvs-physio-1:vfc.q: A 25-year-old woman receives spinal anesthesia for surgery and becomes hypotensive. On a cardiac/vascular function curve diagram, her new operating point reflects:
o: Lower MSFP with lower CO and lower RAP
Higher inotropy with higher CO and lower RAP
Higher TPR with lower CO and higher RAP
Lower inotropy with lower CO and higher RAP
cvs-physio-1:vfc.e: Sympathetic block lowers venous tone → VR curve shifts left → lower CO and RAP.

cvs-physio-1:compl.q: Systemic veins act as blood reservoirs mainly because, compared with arteries, they have greater:
cvs-physio-1:compl.e: Venous compliance is ~24 times arterial compliance.

cvs-physio-1:compl.q: Age-related stiffening of the aorta typically causes:
o: Lower systolic pressure and wider pulse pressure
Higher diastolic pressure and narrower pulse pressure
Higher systolic pressure and wider pulse pressure
Lower diastolic pressure and narrower pulse pressure
cvs-physio-1:compl.e: Reduced compliance → isolated systolic hypertension in older adults.

cvs-physio-1:compl.q: During BP measurement in a woman with dyspnea and JVD, systolic pressure falls by 16 mm Hg on inspiration. This finding is called:
cvs-physio-1:compl.e: An inspiratory fall in systolic pressure > 10 mm Hg; classic in cardiac tamponade.

cvs-physio-1:pvloop.q: On a left ventricular PV loop, the period of highest myocardial O₂ consumption is:
cvs-physio-1:pvloop.e: Tension rises sharply while all valves are closed.

cvs-physio-1:pvloop.q: If contractility and preload are constant, an increase in afterload makes the PV loop:
o: Taller and narrower, with higher ESV
Shorter and narrower, with lower EDV
Wider and shorter, with lower ESV
cvs-physio-1:pvloop.e: The ventricle stops ejecting at a higher end-systolic pressure on the same ESPVR → ESV ↑, SV ↓.

cvs-physio-1:pvloop.q: A patient in septic shock receives norepinephrine, and arterial pressure rises from 60 to 85 mm Hg mean. Which change in the LV pressure–volume loop is expected if contractility and EDV are unchanged?
cvs-physio-1:pvloop.e: Higher afterload on the same ESPVR raises ESV and lowers SV.

cvs-physio-1:pvloop.q: The slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relation (ESPVR) is used as an index of:
cvs-physio-1:pvloop.e: ESPVR is a relatively load-independent measure of inotropy.

cvs-physio-1:wiggers.q: The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure tracing coincides with:
cvs-physio-1:wiggers.e: Brief backflow snaps the aortic valve shut at the start of isovolumetric relaxation.

o: Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole
cvs-physio-1:wiggers.e: S3 follows mitral opening during rapid filling; S4 coincides with the atrial kick.

cvs-physio-1:wiggers.q: A 72-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and LVH has a low-pitched sound heard at the apex just before S1. This sound is lost when she develops atrial fibrillation because it depends on:
o: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle
Ejection through a stiff aortic valve
cvs-physio-1:wiggers.e: S4 requires an effective atrial kick into a noncompliant LV.

cvs-physio-1:jvp.q: The c wave of the jugular venous pulse is caused by:
o: Right atrial emptying after the tricuspid valve opens
Bulging of the closed tricuspid valve during RV contraction
Venous filling of the right atrium during systole
Right atrial contraction against an open tricuspid valve
cvs-physio-1:jvp.e: c wave = RV isovolumetric contraction pushing the tricuspid leaflets toward the RA.

cvs-physio-1:jvp.q: Absent a waves in the jugular venous pulse are characteristic of:
cvs-physio-1:jvp.e: Without organized atrial contraction there is no a wave.

cvs-physio-1:jvp.q: A man with a wide-complex tachycardia at 170/min has intermittent large waves in his neck veins that do not match the arterial pulse. These waves suggest:
o: Tricuspid regurgitation, favoring right heart failure
cvs-physio-1:jvp.e: Cannon a waves = atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, typical of AV dissociation in VT.

cvs-physio-1:jvp.q: A woman with a history of tuberculosis has edema, ascites, a JVP that rises on inspiration and a prominent, steep y descent. The most likely diagnosis is:
cvs-physio-1:jvp.e: Kussmaul sign plus a deep y descent; in tamponade the y descent is absent.

cvs-physio-1:pvvalve.q: In chronic aortic regurgitation, the left ventricular PV loop shows:
o: Decreased EDV and a decreased stroke volume
A narrow loop shifted toward the left
Increased ESV with a normal EDV
Increased EDV and no true isovolumetric phases
cvs-physio-1:pvvalve.e: Backflow during diastole raises EDV; the ventricle never has all valves closed.

cvs-physio-1:pvvalve.q: Which valvular lesion decreases both end-diastolic volume and stroke volume?

A 78-year-old man with exertional syncope has a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Catheterization shows LV systolic pressure 210 mm Hg and aortic systolic pressure 120 mm Hg. Compared with normal, his LV PV loop shows:
o: Lower ESV with a wider loop
Higher EDV with no isovolumetric phases
Higher peak pressure with increased ESV
Lower EDV with lower peak pressure
cvs-physio-1:pvvalve.e: Aortic stenosis: LV pressure ≫ aortic, ESV ↑, SV ↓.

cvs-physio-1:split.q: Physiologic splitting of S2 widens during inspiration because:
o: Decreased venous return shortens LV ejection
Aortic valve closure is delayed by inspiration
Increased venous return prolongs RV ejection
cvs-physio-1:split.e: More RV filling → longer RV ejection → later P2 (pulmonary impedance also falls).

cvs-physio-1:split.q: Fixed splitting of S2 is classically heard with:
cvs-physio-1:split.e: The left-to-right shunt keeps RV volume high in both phases of respiration.

cvs-physio-1:split.q: A 64-year-old man has severe aortic stenosis. On auscultation, S2 is split during expiration and becomes single during inspiration. The best explanation is:
o: Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve
Delayed closure of the aortic valve
cvs-physio-1:split.e: Paradoxical splitting: A2 follows P2; inspiration delays P2 toward A2.

cvs-physio-1:ausc.q: A murmur that becomes louder with the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver is most consistent with:
cvs-physio-1:ausc.e: Less preload → smaller LV cavity → more outflow obstruction.

cvs-physio-1:ausc.q: Hand grip increases the intensity of the murmur of:
cvs-physio-1:ausc.e: Higher afterload increases regurgitant flow (MR, AR, VSD).

cvs-physio-1:ausc.q: A 19-year-old athlete has a systolic murmur at the left sternal border that softens when he squats and gets louder when he stands. The murmur most likely reflects:
o: Stenosis of a bicuspid aortic valve
cvs-physio-1:ausc.e: HCM murmurs increase as LV volume falls (standing, Valsalva) and decrease as it rises (squatting).

cvs-physio-1:murmurs.q: A continuous machine-like murmur heard best in the left infraclavicular area suggests:
cvs-physio-1:murmurs.e: PDA flow persists in systole and diastole, peaking at S2.

cvs-physio-1:murmurs.q: In mitral stenosis, a shorter interval between S2 and the opening snap indicates:
cvs-physio-1:murmurs.e: Higher LA pressure opens the valve earlier.

cvs-physio-1:murmurs.q: A 34-year-old woman from a country with endemic rheumatic fever has dyspnea and hemoptysis. There is a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex after an opening snap. Which complication is she most at risk for?
o: Fixed splitting of S2 from an atrial shunt
Left ventricular hypertrophy from pressure overload
Pulsus parvus et tardus from outflow obstruction
Atrial fibrillation from left atrial enlargement
cvs-physio-1:murmurs.e: Mitral stenosis dilates the LA → AF, thrombus, Ortner syndrome.

cvs-physio-1:murmurs.q: A 66-year-old man has an early diastolic decrescendo murmur, bounding pulses and head bobbing with each heartbeat. Which finding is also expected?
cvs-physio-1:murmurs.e: Aortic regurgitation: high SV and low diastolic pressure.

cvs-physio-2:apv.q: The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is maintained mainly by:
o: Na⁺ influx through fast channels balanced by Cl⁻ influx
K⁺ influx through inward rectifiers balanced by Na⁺ efflux
Ca²⁺ release from the SR balanced by Na⁺ influx
Ca²⁺ influx through L-type channels balanced by K⁺ efflux
cvs-physio-2:apv.e: L-type Ca²⁺ inward current is offset by delayed-rectifier K⁺ outward current.

cvs-physio-2:apv.q: Phase 0 of the ventricular myocyte action potential is due to:
o: Opening of voltage-gated L-type Ca²⁺ channels
Opening of voltage-gated fast Na⁺ channels
cvs-physio-2:apv.e: Fast Na⁺ current produces the rapid upstroke in atrial, ventricular and Purkinje cells.

cvs-physio-2:apv.q: Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized by rapid repetitive stimulation. The main reason is that:
o: Its effective refractory period lasts almost as long as contraction
It depends on gap junctions to spread excitation between cells
Its thin filaments lack troponin C, so Ca²⁺ cannot bind
Its resting membrane potential is much less negative than skeletal
cvs-physio-2:apv.e: The long plateau extends refractoriness through most of the twitch.

cvs-physio-2:app.q: Spontaneous phase 4 depolarization of SA nodal cells is mainly due to:
o: The funny current (I_f) through HCN channels
cvs-physio-2:app.e: I_f is a mixed Na⁺/K⁺ inward current activated by hyperpolarization.

cvs-physio-2:app.q: The upstroke of the SA nodal action potential is slow because:
o: The HCN channels close abruptly at the start of phase 0
Nodal cells lack any voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the membrane
Nodal cells have no functioning K⁺ channels during phase 3
Fast Na⁺ channels are inactivated at the nodal resting potential
cvs-physio-2:app.e: At −55 to −60 mV most fast Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so phase 0 relies on Ca²⁺ current.

cvs-physio-2:app.q: A 30-year-old woman with paroxysmal SVT receives IV adenosine and her heart rate falls abruptly. In SA and AV nodal cells, adenosine acts by:
o: Increasing K⁺ conductance and lowering the phase 4 slope
Prolonging the plateau through more Ca²⁺ entry
Blocking fast Na⁺ channels and slowing phase 0
Increasing cAMP and opening more HCN channels
cvs-physio-2:app.e: Like ACh, adenosine activates K⁺ channels → hyperpolarization and slower diastolic depolarization.

cvs-physio-2:ecg.q: The PR interval mainly reflects conduction delay in the:
cvs-physio-2:ecg.e: Normal PR 120–200 ms; most of it is AV nodal delay.

cvs-physio-2:ecg.q: Prominent U waves on the ECG are most associated with:
The AV node of a 59-year-old man with an inferior STEMI and new second-degree AV block is most likely supplied by the:
cvs-physio-2:ecg.e: The AV node blood supply is via the PDA (from the RCA in right-dominant hearts).

cvs-physio-2:ecg.q: Rank conduction velocity from fastest to slowest:

cvs-physio-2:refr.q: During the effective refractory period, a second stimulus fails to produce a propagated action potential because:
o: The membrane is hyperpolarized below E_K
Gap junctions are closed during the plateau
Most fast Na⁺ channels are still inactivated
cvs-physio-2:refr.e: Na⁺ channels must recover (repolarize) before they can reopen.

cvs-physio-2:refr.q: A stimulus delivered in the relative refractory period of a ventricular cell produces an action potential that is:
o: Larger, with a faster upstroke and conduction
Identical to a normal action potential
Smaller, with a slower upstroke and conduction
cvs-physio-2:refr.e: Only part of the Na⁺ channels have recovered.

cvs-physio-2:refr.q: A premature impulse reaches tissue where one pathway is still refractory and the other has recovered, setting up a reentrant circuit. A drug that lengthens the effective refractory period helps terminate it because:
o: Automaticity of the SA node increases
The resting membrane potential becomes more negative
The returning impulse meets tissue that is still refractory
The impulse is conducted faster around the circuit
cvs-physio-2:refr.e: Prolonging ERP removes the excitable gap so the circulating wave dies out.

cvs-physio-2:ecgread.q: On a standard ECG at 25 mm/s, one small (1 mm) box represents:
The QRS is positive in lead I and negative in aVF. The axis is most likely:
cvs-physio-2:ecgread.e: Positive I and negative aVF place the axis between 0° and −90° (LAD if beyond −30°).

cvs-physio-2:ecgread.q: A 25-year-old man with long-standing pulmonic stenosis has a tall R in V1. His QRS is negative in lead I and positive in aVF. This axis pattern most likely reflects:
o: Normal conduction in a young adult
cvs-physio-2:ecgread.e: RVH shifts the mean QRS vector rightward (I negative, aVF positive).

cvs-physio-2:natri.q: ANP exerts its effects through which second messenger?
cvs-physio-2:natri.e: Natriuretic peptide receptors are guanylyl cyclases.

o: Dilating afferent and constricting efferent arterioles
Constricting afferent and dilating efferent arterioles
Increasing plasma oncotic pressure in the glomerulus
Increasing renin and angiotensin II release
cvs-physio-2:natri.e: Both changes raise glomerular capillary pressure.

cvs-physio-2:natri.q: A 67-year-old man presents with dyspnea. A low plasma BNP level in this setting is most useful because it:
o: Makes heart failure an unlikely cause of the dyspnea
Predicts a good response to loop diuretics
Indicates that atrial pressure is markedly elevated
Confirms heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
cvs-physio-2:natri.e: BNP has a very high negative predictive value for HF.

cvs-physio-2:baro.q: Afferent signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla in the:
cvs-physio-2:baro.e: Carotid sinus → Hering nerve → CN IX → NTS; aortic arch → CN X.

cvs-physio-2:baro.q: Central chemoreceptors respond primarily to changes in:
o: Mean arterial blood pressure in the carotids
PO₂ of arterial blood perfusing the brain
PCO₂ and pH of brain interstitial fluid
Plasma K⁺ concentration in arterial blood
cvs-physio-2:baro.e: CO₂ crosses the BBB; H⁺ does not; PO₂ does not stimulate central chemoreceptors.

cvs-physio-2:baro.q: An 80-year-old man faints while shaving. ECG during carotid massage shows sinus pauses. The mechanism of his syncope is:
o: Decreased baroreceptor firing causing sympathetic surge
Increased baroreceptor firing causing vagal bradycardia
cvs-physio-2:baro.e: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: pressure on the sinus mimics hypertension.

cvs-physio-2:baro.q: A man with a large epidural hematoma has BP 210/110 mm Hg, HR 44/min and irregular breathing. The bradycardia is caused by:
o: Baroreceptor response to the central pressor reflex
Direct compression of the SA nodal artery
cvs-physio-2:baro.e: Cushing reflex: cerebral ischemia → sympathetic HTN → baroreflex bradycardia.

cvs-physio-2:press.q: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure overestimates left ventricular end-diastolic pressure in:
cvs-physio-2:press.e: The stenotic mitral valve creates a gradient between LA (≈PCWP) and LV.

cvs-physio-2:press.q: Normal right ventricular pressure is closest to:

A patient in shock has a pulmonary artery catheter placed. When the balloon is inflated, the tracing changes from 42/26 to a damped waveform with a mean of 24 mm Hg. Assuming no valve disease, this value best estimates:
cvs-physio-2:press.e: PCWP reflects LA pressure (normal 4–12); 24 mm Hg suggests a cardiogenic cause.

cvs-physio-2:longbp.q: In the long term, mean arterial pressure is set mainly by:
o: The renal output curve for salt and water
The heart rate set by the SA node
cvs-physio-2:longbp.e: Pressure natriuresis returns MAP to the equilibrium point where output = intake.

cvs-physio-2:longbp.q: Arterial baroreceptors are poor regulators of long-term blood pressure because they:
o: Respond only to pressures below 60 mm Hg
Cannot alter heart rate or vascular tone
Reset to a sustained new pressure within days
cvs-physio-2:longbp.e: Baroreceptor adaptation limits their long-term role.

cvs-physio-2:longbp.q: A man with primary hyperaldosteronism cannot suppress aldosterone when he eats more salt. Compared with a healthy person, a high-salt diet in this patient raises arterial pressure:
o: Not at all, because ANP fully compensates
Much less, because his renal output curve is steeper
Much more, because his renal output curve is flatter
cvs-physio-2:longbp.e: Without RAAS suppression, the renal function curve is shifted and flattened → salt-sensitive BP.

cvs-physio-2:autoreg.e: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood to ventilated alveoli.

cvs-physio-2:autoreg.q: Cerebral blood flow is regulated mostly by:
cvs-physio-2:autoreg.e: Hypercapnia dilates; hyperventilation constricts cerebral vessels.

cvs-physio-2:autoreg.q: A man with raised intracranial pressure after head trauma is briefly hyperventilated. Intracranial pressure falls because:
cvs-physio-2:autoreg.e: Hypocapnia → cerebral vasoconstriction → less cerebral blood volume.

cvs-physio-2:autoreg.q: During heavy exercise, blood flow to skeletal muscle rises mainly because of:
o: Increased circulating angiotensin II and vasopressin
A myogenic response to raised arterial pressure
Increased sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone to muscle
Local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺, adenosine, lactate, K⁺)
cvs-physio-2:autoreg.e: CHALK metabolites override sympathetic tone during exercise.

cvs-physio-2:starlingf.q: Which change promotes net fluid movement out of capillaries?
cvs-physio-2:starlingf.e: πi pulls fluid out; πc and Pi oppose filtration.

cvs-physio-2:starlingf.q: The reflection coefficient (σ) in the Starling equation describes:
o: The hydrostatic gradient across the wall
The surface area available for filtration
How impermeable the capillary wall is to protein
How permeable the capillary wall is to water
cvs-physio-2:starlingf.e: σ = 1 means proteins cannot cross; σ near 0 means they cross freely.

cvs-physio-2:starlingf.q: A 48-year-old woman has periorbital and leg edema, serum albumin 1.8 g/dL and urine protein 6 g/day. Her edema is primarily due to:

cvs-physio-2:edema.q: Edema after radical mastectomy with axillary node dissection is due mainly to:
cvs-physio-2:edema.e: Lymphatic removal lets protein accumulate in the interstitium.

cvs-physio-2:edema.q: Which factor helps protect tissues against edema when capillary pressure rises?
cvs-physio-2:edema.e: Lymph flow, low interstitial compliance and protein washdown form safety factors.

cvs-physio-2:edema.q: A man with severe burns over 40% of his body develops widespread edema despite normal heart function. The main cause is:
cvs-physio-2:edema.e: Burns raise Kf and let protein escape.

cvs-physio-2:coronary.q: Blood flow in the left coronary artery is greatest during:
cvs-physio-2:coronary.e: Systolic compression of intramyocardial vessels limits LV flow.

cvs-physio-2:coronary.q: The region of the left ventricle most vulnerable to ischemia is the:
cvs-physio-2:coronary.e: It is most compressed in systole and farthest from epicardial vessels.

cvs-physio-2:coronary.q: A 56-year-old man with coronary stenosis has angina only when his heart rate exceeds 120/min. Tachycardia worsens his ischemia mainly because it:
o: Shortens diastole, when most LV perfusion occurs
Reduces myocardial O₂ demand per minute
Lengthens systole, when most LV perfusion occurs
cvs-physio-2:coronary.e: Higher HR raises demand and cuts diastolic perfusion time.

title.en: Boss case: Breathless with swollen legs

boss.case: A 64-year-old man with prior MI has 3 months of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea and ankle edema. BP 128/78 mm Hg, HR 92, bibasal crackles, JVP raised. Echocardiogram: LVEF 30%. eGFR 60, K⁺ 4.3.

qs.q: Drug that relieves his congestion fastest:
qs.e: Loops relieve symptoms but do not improve survival.

qs.q: Which combination forms the core mortality-reducing therapy for HFrEF?
qs.e: The four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy: ARNI (or ACEi/ARB), an evidence-based β-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Combined with valsartan; never with an ACE inhibitor (angioedema).

qs.q: Which β-blocker is NOT proven for HFrEF?
qs.e: Only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol reduce mortality.

qs.q: A key lab to monitor after starting spironolactone:
qs.e: Hyperkalemia risk, especially with ACEi/ARNI and CKD.

qs.q: If he remains symptomatic in sinus rhythm with EF ≤ 35%, digoxin can:
o: Reverse LV remodeling and improve survival
Replace the need for loop diuretics
qs.e: Digoxin improves symptoms and reduces admissions only.

stem.en: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has 2 days of palpitations; pulse 130 irregular, BP 128/80.

steps.q: Drug for rate control in a stable patient with normal EF:
o: Adenosine as a repeated IV bolus
steps.e: β-blockers and non-DHP CCBs slow AV nodal conduction.

steps.q: Diltiazem slows AV conduction by blocking:

steps.e: DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF.

stem.th: ชาย 62 ปี สูบบุหรี่ เบาหวาน เจ็บแน่นหน้าอกร้าวไปแขนซ้าย 40 นาที เหงื่อแตก
stem.en: A 62-year-old smoker with diabetes has 40 minutes of crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm, with sweating.

steps.q: The occluded artery is most likely the:
steps.e: Inferior leads II, III and aVF usually map to the RCA (right-dominant circulation).

info.th: ECG: ST ยกใน II, III, aVF
info.en: ECG: ST elevation in II, III and aVF

steps.e: Hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs with inferior STEMI suggest RV infarction; avoid nitrates and give fluids.

info.th: ความดัน 84/50 JVP สูง ปอดใส

steps.q: At 12 hours, biopsy of the infarct would show:
o: Dense collagen scar with few cells
steps.e: Neutrophils arrive within about 12–24 h; macrophages at 3–7 days; granulation tissue at 1–2 weeks; scar by 2 months.
Papillary muscle rupture (often posteromedial, supplied by the RCA) occurs at 2–7 days and causes acute mitral regurgitation.

stem.th: ชาย 78 ปี หน้ามืดเป็นลมขณะเดินขึ้นเนิน 2 ครั้ง และเจ็บหน้าอกเวลาออกแรง
stem.en: A 78-year-old man has fainted twice while walking uphill and gets chest pain on exertion.

steps.q: The pulse would most likely be:
o: Slow-rising and weak (pulsus parvus et tardus)
Bounding with a wide pulse pressure
steps.e: Fixed outflow obstruction delays and dampens the carotid upstroke.

info.th: ฟังได้ crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur ที่ RUSB ร้าวไปคอ
info.en: Crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids

steps.q: Compared with normal, his LV pressure–volume loop shows:
o: A wide loop with no isovolumetric phases
A shift to the left with low pressures
steps.e: The LV must generate far higher pressure than the aorta to eject through the stenotic valve.

steps.q: The underlying process is best described as:
steps.e: Calcific aortic stenosis in the elderly is dystrophic calcification of a normal trileaflet valve; a bicuspid valve presents earlier.

info.th: Echo: valve มีหินปูนหนา ลิ้นสามแผ่น

steps.q: The LV adapts to the chronic pressure load with:
o: Dilatation with a thin, compliant wall
steps.e: Pressure overload adds sarcomeres in parallel, thickening the wall; volume overload causes eccentric hypertrophy.

clues: Turns blue when crying and squats after running
Lips cyanotic, harsh systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border
CXR: boot-shaped heart with reduced lung markings
Echo: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow stenosis, RVH
dx.e: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum; RV outflow obstruction drives the right-to-left shunt.

clues: Short stature and widely spaced nipples
BP 172/94 mm Hg in arms; legs cold
CXR: notching of the inferior rib margins
MRI: narrowing just distal to the left subclavian artery
dx.e: Turner syndrome association; intercostal collaterals erode the ribs.

clues: Murmur noted in childhood, never treated
Echo: large VSD with right-to-left flow, severe pulmonary hypertension
dx.e: Long-standing left-to-right shunt remodels pulmonary arterioles until the shunt reverses.

clues: Severe headache and vomiting for a day
Kidney biopsy: onion-skin arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis
dx.e: Severe hypertension with acute organ damage; lower MAP gradually with IV agents.

clues: Sudden severe back and flank pain
Tender pulsatile mass above the umbilicus
Surgery: retroperitoneal hematoma around a ruptured aneurysm
dx.e: Transmural inflammation and matrix degradation; smoking is the strongest risk factor.

clues: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back
CT angiography: intimal flap in the ascending aorta
dx.e: Intimal tear with false lumen in the media; type A needs emergency surgery.

clues: Painful purple toes; pedal pulses palpable
Skin biopsy: biconvex needle-shaped clefts in arterioles
dx.e: Atheromatous debris showers small arteries after vascular procedures.

clues: Woke with heavy epigastric pressure and nausea
ECG: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with ST depression in I and aVL
dx.e: RCA occlusion; RV involvement makes the patient preload-dependent.

clues: Chest pain wakes her at 5 a.m.
Pain resolves within 15 minutes; none with exercise
Angiography: normal arteries; spasm induced by provocation
dx.e: Coronary spasm at rest; treat with CCBs and nitrates, stop smoking.

clues: New holosystolic murmur at the apex
Pink frothy sputum, BP 80/50 mm Hg
dx.e: Posteromedial papillary muscle has single PDA supply.
Autoimmune pericarditis weeks after cardiac injury.

clues: Slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave)
dx.e: Accessory pathway; avoid AV nodal blockers if AF occurs; ablation is curative.

clues: Nocturnal agonal breathing witnessed by his wife
Brother died suddenly in his sleep
Coved ST elevation in V1–V2 · Na⁺ channel mutation
dx.e: Autosomal dominant Na⁺ channelopathy; ICD prevents sudden death.

clues: Sudden right arm weakness that resolved
ECG: no discernible P waves, irregular RR intervals
dx.e: LA appendage thrombus embolized; calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc and anticoagulate.

clues: Systolic murmur that gets louder with Valsalva
Echo: asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
dx.e: Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation; avoid preload reduction; ICD if high risk.
Systolic dysfunction with eccentric hypertrophy; alcohol is a reversible cause.

clues: Distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Systolic BP falls 16 mm Hg on inspiration
ECG: low voltage with electrical alternans
dx.e: Equalized diastolic pressures; urgent pericardiocentesis.
Rigid pericardium limits filling; Kussmaul sign.

clues: High fever and rigors for 5 days
Holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration
Blood cultures: Staphylococcus aureus in 3 of 3 bottles
dx.e: Right-sided S. aureus endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.

clues: Painful swollen joints that move from knee to ankle to wrist
Pink rings on the trunk that come and go
dx.e: J♥NES after group A strep pharyngitis; molecular mimicry against myosin.

clues: Fever, weight loss and fatigue for months
Echo: pedunculated mass attached to the fossa ovalis
dx.e: Most common primary cardiac tumor in adults; ball-valve obstruction.

clues: New headache over the left temple
Pain in the jaw when chewing
Shoulder and hip stiffness in the mornings
Biopsy: granulomatous inflammation with giant cells fragmenting the internal elastic lamina
dx.e: Start steroids immediately to prevent blindness.

clues: Fever, night sweats and joint pain
Angiography: stenoses of aortic arch branches
dx.e: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of young Asian women.

clues: Fever, weight loss, abdominal pain after eating
New hypertension and left foot drop
Angiography: microaneurysms in renal and mesenteric arteries
dx.e: Transmural necrotizing vasculitis of medium arteries; spares lungs.

clues: Fever for 6 days not responding to antibiotics
Swollen hands and feet; cervical node 2 cm
dx.e: Medium-vessel vasculitis of children; IVIG + aspirin.

clues: Chronic sinusitis and bloody nasal crusts
dx.e: Necrotizing granulomas of airways, vasculitis and pauci-immune GN.

clues: Raised purple spots on buttocks and legs
Colicky abdominal pain · stool guaiac positive
dx.e: IgA immune complex small-vessel vasculitis; most common childhood vasculitis.

clues: Fingers turn white then blue in the cold
Painful ulcer on the tip of a toe
Tender red cord along a superficial vein
Angiography: segmental occlusion of distal arteries, corkscrew collaterals
dx.e: Segmental thrombosing vasculitis; smoking cessation is essential.
